_about: Country-specific facts for the indexable learn-hindi-from-* pages (AdSense plan P3 / D-20, 29 Sep 2026). Applied by tools/apply-country-specifics.py. Time-zone and daylight-saving facts are as of 2026 (Iran dropped DST in 2022, Jordan and Syria moved to permanent UTC+3 in 2022, Kazakhstan unified on UTC+5 in March 2024, Türkiye has kept UTC+3 all year since 2016). 'dst' is null when the country does not change its clocks; otherwise it names the summer period. 'zones' is null for a single-zone country.

afghanistan.hook: Kabul runs its clocks on the half hour, at UTC+4:30, which puts it just one hour behind Delhi — close enough that an evening lesson in India is an evening lesson in Afghanistan too.
afghanistan.script: Dari and Pashto are written in a Perso-Arabic script, right to left; Devanagari runs left to right and hangs its letters from a line along the top, so the script is genuinely new — but a lot of the vocabulary written in it will not be.
afghanistan.fl: Dari speakers start with a real vocabulary advantage: hundreds of everyday Hindi words — dost, zindagi, kitab, shukriya — came from Persian and are still in daily use.

armenia.hook: Armenia sits at UTC+4 and has not changed its clocks since 2012, so the gap to India is a steady hour and a half all year — no spring or autumn surprises in a lesson schedule.
armenia.script: Armenian has its own alphabet, written left to right like Devanagari; the new idea is that Devanagari vowels after a consonant are written as small marks attached to it rather than as full letters.
armenia.fl: Armenian and Hindi are distant cousins in the Indo-European family, which shows in a few old shared roots, but in practice the useful carry-over is Armenian's own aspirated consonants — the difference between p and ph that English speakers struggle to hear.

azerbaijan.hook: Azerbaijan dropped daylight saving in 2016 and stays at UTC+4, an hour and a half behind India, which makes a lesson before work in Baku an early-afternoon lesson for the tutor.
azerbaijan.script: Azerbaijani is written in a Latin alphabet today (Cyrillic before 1991); Devanagari is a different system in which each consonant carries a built-in a-sound that a small vowel mark can change.
azerbaijan.fl: Azerbaijani borrowed heavily from Persian and Arabic, and so did Hindi — kitab, dünya and xəbər (khabar in Hindi) turn up on both sides, which gives vocabulary a head start.

bahrain.hook: A tutor's 9 a.m. in India is 6:30 in the morning in Manama, so Bahraini learners can fit a lesson in before work, and the last evening slots finish around 7:30 p.m. local time.
bahrain.script: Arabic is written right to left and mostly without short vowels; Devanagari writes every vowel and runs left to right, which Arabic readers usually find easier than they expect once the direction flips.
bahrain.fl: Arabic speakers already produce the deep kh and gh sounds that Urdu-flavoured Hindi uses in words like khush and ghazal, and a long list of words — kitab, waqt, duniya — is shared.

bangladesh.hook: Bangladesh is half an hour ahead of India at UTC+6, and Bengali and Hindi share a common ancestor — many learners in Dhaka already follow Hindi films and songs before a first lesson.
bangladesh.script: The Bengali script is a sister of Devanagari: the same consonant order, vowel signs that attach to consonants, and a line along the top. Many letters look related, so reading comes quickly.
bangladesh.fl: Bengali speakers recognise much of Hindi's core vocabulary from shared Sanskrit roots; the main adjustments are Hindi's grammatical gender, which Bengali does not have, and the a-sound that Bengali rounds towards o.

bhutan.hook: In Thimphu the tutors' day runs from 9:30 in the morning to 10:30 at night, and because the ngultrum is pegged one-to-one to the rupee, the price of a lesson is easy to reckon.
bhutan.script: Dzongkha is written in the Tibetan script, which descends from the same Brahmi family as Devanagari: the consonant order (ka, kha, ga, nga) and the idea of vowel marks around a consonant will look familiar.
bhutan.fl: Nepali speakers in southern Bhutan have the easiest start of anyone outside India — Nepali uses Devanagari and shares a large share of Hindi's vocabulary.

brunei.hook: Brunei sits at UTC+8, two and a half hours ahead of India, so a tutor's morning in India is lunchtime in Bandar Seri Begawan and a tutor's evening is well into the night.
brunei.script: Malay is written in Latin letters and also in Jawi, an Arabic-based script; Devanagari is neither, but its sound-by-sound spelling is closer to Malay's regular spelling than English is.
brunei.fl: Malay borrowed words from Sanskrit centuries ago — bahasa, raja, guru, bumi — and many of them are still recognisable in Hindi, which surprises most Malay-speaking learners.

cambodia.hook: Cambodia is at UTC+7, an hour and a half ahead of India, and Khmer carries a deep layer of Sanskrit and Pali from the Angkor period that makes some Hindi words feel oddly familiar.
cambodia.script: Khmer script comes from the same Brahmi family as Devanagari: consonants in the same order and vowels written as signs around a consonant. The shapes differ, but the logic is the one you already read.
cambodia.fl: Khmer speakers recognise learned words that came from Sanskrit; the new parts are Hindi's verb-at-the-end order and verb endings that change with gender.

canada.dst: from the second Sunday of March to the first Sunday of November (most provinces; most of Saskatchewan and all of Yukon keep one time all year)
canada.zones: Canada spans six time zones, from Newfoundland (UTC-3:30) to the Pacific coast (UTC-8); the figures here are Eastern Time, so a learner in Vancouver should subtract three hours.
canada.hook: From Toronto the tutors' day starts at 10:30 the evening before and ends at 11:30 in the morning, so most Canadian learners book either late at night or before lunch — the booking page does that arithmetic for every province.
canada.script: Canadian learners read a Latin alphabet; Devanagari is phonetic, so once its 44 or so letters are learned every word can be read aloud exactly as written — unlike English or French spelling.
canada.fl: English and French speakers both need to train their ears for the retroflex t and d and for aspiration, which Hindi uses to tell words apart; French speakers get a head start on Hindi's nasal vowels.

ethiopia.hook: Ethiopia keeps UTC+3 all year — but many people also count hours from dawn in Ethiopian local time, so it is worth confirming a lesson in the booking page's international clock rather than by word of mouth.
ethiopia.script: Amharic's Ge'ez script (fidel) is an abugida, exactly like Devanagari: each character is a consonant with a vowel built in, and the vowel is changed by modifying the character. Ethiopian learners often find Devanagari's logic the most familiar part of Hindi.
ethiopia.fl: Amharic speakers already use ejective and pharyngeal sounds that English lacks, so Hindi's aspirated and retroflex consonants are less of a hurdle; the vocabulary, though, starts mostly from zero.

georgia.hook: Georgia has stayed at UTC+4 since 2005 with no clock changes, so a lesson booked with a tutor in India an hour and a half ahead keeps the same local time in January and July.
georgia.script: Georgian has its own unique alphabet (Mkhedruli), written left to right with no capital letters — much like Devanagari, which also has no capitals. The difference is that Devanagari attaches vowels to consonants as marks.
georgia.fl: Georgian speakers already distinguish aspirated from ejective consonants, a three-way contrast that makes Hindi's aspirated pairs (k/kh, p/ph) easier to hear than they are for English speakers.

haiti.dst: from the second Sunday of March to the first Sunday of November
haiti.hook: Haiti is ten and a half hours behind India in winter, so the tutors' working day falls across Haiti's night and early morning — early risers have the most choice of slots.
haiti.script: Haitian Creole and French use the Latin alphabet; Creole's spelling is phonetic, one letter per sound, which is exactly how Devanagari works too.
haiti.fl: French and Creole speakers already have nasal vowels, which Hindi uses in words like main (I) and hain (are); the retroflex consonants are the part that needs deliberate practice.

india.hook: Learning Hindi from inside India usually means a specific goal — a move to a Hindi-speaking city, a workplace, a partner's family — and the tutors share your clock, so any hour of the teaching day is available.
india.script: If you went to school in India you may already read Devanagari from Hindi, Marathi, Sanskrit or Nepali classes; if your first language uses another Indian script, the letters follow the same order, so learning Devanagari is mostly learning new shapes.
india.fl: Speakers of other Indian languages share a great deal of vocabulary and the retroflex sounds with Hindi; the adjustments are usually gender agreement and the ne construction in the past tense.

indonesia.zones: Indonesia has three zones — WIB (UTC+7) for Java and Sumatra, WITA (UTC+8) for Bali and Sulawesi, and WIT (UTC+9) for Maluku and Papua; the figures here are WIB, so add one hour in Bali and two in Papua.
indonesia.hook: In Jakarta the tutors' teaching day runs from 10:30 in the morning to 11:30 at night, so an after-work lesson at seven or eight in the evening is the easiest slot to find.
indonesia.script: Indonesian uses the Latin alphabet with very regular spelling; Devanagari is regular too, and it descends from the same Brahmi family as the old Javanese and Balinese scripts.
indonesia.fl: Indonesian has no grammatical gender and no verb endings, so those are the real work in Hindi; the Sanskrit vocabulary Indonesian already contains is the real gift.

iran.hook: Iran abolished daylight saving in 2022 and now stays at UTC+3:30, two hours behind India all year — and Persian's centuries at the Mughal court mean Hindi is full of words an Iranian learner already knows.
iran.script: Persian is written in an Arabic-based script from right to left; Devanagari runs left to right and writes every vowel, so reading is new but spelling is more predictable than in Persian.
iran.fl: Persian speakers recognise a remarkable amount: dost, shahar, zindagi, khabar, bazaar and hundreds more entered Hindi through Persian, and the ezafe-like phrases of Urdu-flavoured Hindi feel natural.

iraq.hook: Iraq has kept UTC+3 without daylight saving since 2008, two and a half hours behind India, so the whole Indian teaching day fits into Iraq's morning and afternoon.
iraq.script: Arabic and Kurdish (in its Sorani form) are written right to left in Arabic script; Devanagari is left to right and hangs letters from a top line, a switch most Iraqi learners manage within a couple of weeks.
iraq.fl: Arabic speakers already produce the sounds behind Hindi words like khabar, ghareeb and qaanoon, and share a good stock of vocabulary that travelled to Hindi through Persian.

israel.dst: from the Friday before the last Sunday of March to the last Sunday of October (UTC+3)
israel.hook: Israel has a steady interest in India through travel after military service and through Indian Jewish communities, and at UTC+2 in winter the Indian teaching day covers Israel's whole morning and afternoon.
israel.script: Hebrew is written right to left and usually without vowels; Devanagari runs left to right and always writes the vowel, which makes it easier to sound out than unpointed Hebrew.
israel.fl: Hebrew speakers already have the guttural kh sound used in Urdu-flavoured Hindi; the retroflex consonants and grammatical gender on verbs (familiar from Hebrew) are the main areas to work on.

jordan.hook: Jordan moved to permanent UTC+3 in 2022, so the gap to India is two and a half hours every day of the year and a lesson slot never drifts with the seasons.
jordan.script: Arabic runs right to left and often leaves short vowels unwritten; Devanagari runs left to right and writes all vowels, so once the direction is familiar Hindi words can be read exactly as they sound.
jordan.fl: Arabic speakers find a shared layer of vocabulary — kitab, waqt, hisaab — and already make the kh and gh sounds of Urdu-flavoured Hindi.

kazakhstan.hook: Kazakhstan moved the whole country onto a single zone, UTC+5, in March 2024, so from Almaty to Aktobe a lesson with India is always half an hour behind the tutor's clock.
kazakhstan.script: Kazakh is written in Cyrillic and is moving to a Latin alphabet; Devanagari is a third system in which vowels after a consonant are written as marks attached to it.
kazakhstan.fl: Russian speakers already have palatalised and hard consonants and a free word order; Kazakh speakers share Hindi's verb-at-the-end sentence order, which makes Hindi sentences feel natural to build.

kosovo.dst: from the last Sunday of March to the last Sunday of October (UTC+2)
kosovo.hook: Kosovo is four and a half hours behind India in winter, which puts the tutors' afternoon and evening across Kosovo's morning and midday — convenient for students and remote workers alike.
kosovo.script: Albanian uses a Latin alphabet with very consistent spelling, and Devanagari shares that one-letter-one-sound principle, even though its letters and vowel marks are new.
kosovo.fl: Albanian speakers already use the sound of the Hindi r trill and several consonant clusters English lacks; retroflex consonants and aspiration are the new sounds to learn.

kuwait.hook: In Kuwait City the tutors' day starts at 6:30 in the morning and ends at 7:30 in the evening, which suits learners who can take a lesson before a shift or straight after one.
kuwait.script: Arabic is written right to left in a joined-up script; Devanagari is left to right, with letters joined along a top line, and writes every vowel explicitly.
kuwait.fl: Arabic speakers share words that reached Hindi through Persian — duniya, waqt, kitab — and already produce the kh and q sounds that Urdu-flavoured Hindi keeps.

kyrgyzstan.hook: In Bishkek, lessons can run from 9:30 in the morning to 10:30 at night, half an hour ahead of the tutor's own clock — so a student can fit one around lectures on almost any day.
kyrgyzstan.script: Kyrgyz and Russian are written in Cyrillic; Devanagari is a different kind of system — an abugida — in which each consonant carries a vowel that small marks change.
kyrgyzstan.fl: Kyrgyz, like Hindi, puts the verb at the end of the sentence and uses postpositions instead of prepositions, so Hindi word order feels familiar; Russian speakers bring a good ear for hard and soft consonants.

laos.hook: In Vientiane the tutors' teaching day runs from 10:30 in the morning to 11:30 at night, so a lesson after work or after classes is easy to place.
laos.script: The Lao script belongs to the Brahmi family, like Devanagari: consonants carry vowels written around them, and the consonant order is related. Lao readers recognise the system even where the shapes differ.
laos.fl: Lao is tonal and Hindi is not, so learners can relax about pitch; the work is in Hindi's gender, verb endings and consonant clusters.

lebanon.dst: from the last Sunday of March to the last Sunday of October (UTC+3)
lebanon.hook: Lebanon is three and a half hours behind India in winter, so the tutors' teaching day covers Lebanon's early morning to late afternoon, and summer time pushes every slot an hour later on the Lebanese clock.
lebanon.script: Arabic runs right to left; Devanagari runs left to right and writes every vowel. Lebanese learners who also read French are used to Latin letters, but Devanagari is phonetic in a way French spelling is not.
lebanon.fl: Arabic and French speakers both bring useful sounds: the Arabic kh and gh for Urdu-flavoured Hindi, and French nasal vowels for words like main and hain.

malaysia.hook: In Kuala Lumpur the tutors' day runs from 11:30 in the morning until just after midnight, so an evening lesson after work is easy to book, with the price shown in ringgit as well as dollars.
malaysia.script: Malay is written in Latin letters; Tamil speakers already read a Brahmi-family script, so Devanagari's consonant order and vowel signs are familiar, just with more letters for aspirated sounds.
malaysia.fl: Malay contains Sanskrit words that Hindi still uses — raja, guru, bahasa — and English speakers can lean on the many English loanwords in everyday Hindi.

maldives.hook: The Maldives is only half an hour behind India, at UTC+5, and Hindi films and TV are widely watched there — so a lesson slot means almost the same thing on both clocks.
maldives.script: Dhivehi is written in Thaana, right to left, with vowels as marks over or under consonants; Devanagari also writes vowels as marks on consonants, but runs left to right.
maldives.fl: Dhivehi is an Indo-Aryan language, a relative of Hindi through Sinhala, so some basic vocabulary and many sounds carry over; many Maldivians also pick up spoken Hindi from films.

moldova.dst: from the last Sunday of March to the last Sunday of October (UTC+3)
moldova.hook: In Chișinău the tutors' day starts at 5:30 in the morning in winter (6:30 in summer) and ends in the early evening, so lessons fit around a working or university day.
moldova.script: Romanian is written in Latin letters with consistent spelling (Russian, also widely spoken, uses Cyrillic); Devanagari is consistent too, but vowels after a consonant are written as attached marks.
moldova.fl: Romanian speakers already have a rolled r and the neutral vowel ă, close to Hindi's short a; Russian speakers bring an ear for palatal consonants.

myanmar.hook: Myanmar keeps its own half-hour zone, UTC+6:30, exactly one hour ahead of India, and has old ties to India through Buddhism and a long-settled Indian community in Yangon.
myanmar.script: The Burmese script descends from the Brahmi family, as Devanagari does: consonants carry an inherent vowel and other vowels are written as marks around them — the same idea in rounder shapes.
myanmar.fl: Burmese is tonal and puts the verb at the end, as Hindi does, so Hindi sentence order feels natural; Pali-derived Buddhist vocabulary gives a few familiar words.

nepal.hook: Nepal sets its clocks 15 minutes ahead of India, at UTC+5:45 — one of the few quarter-hour zones in the world — and most Nepalis already understand spoken Hindi from films and television.
nepal.script: Nepali is written in Devanagari, so there is nothing new to learn: every letter, vowel sign and conjunct in Hindi is one you already read.
nepal.fl: Nepali and Hindi share the script and a large part of their vocabulary; the differences are verb endings, a few everyday words and Hindi's two-gender agreement.

new-zealand.dst: from the last Sunday of September to the first Sunday of April (NZDT, UTC+13)
new-zealand.zones: The Chatham Islands keep their own time, 45 minutes ahead of the rest of New Zealand.
new-zealand.hook: New Zealand is the furthest-ahead country with a large Indian community — up to seven and a half hours ahead of India — so a tutor's morning lands in a New Zealand afternoon and a tutor's evening runs past midnight.
new-zealand.script: New Zealand learners read a Latin alphabet; Devanagari is phonetic, and speakers of te reo Māori will recognise the principle of spelling that matches sound exactly.
new-zealand.fl: English speakers can lean on the many English loanwords in everyday Hindi; the work is hearing aspirated and retroflex consonants, which English does not use to separate words.

oman.hook: In Muscat a lesson can start as early as 7:30 in the morning or as late as 8:30 in the evening, which fits around both office hours and the Omani working week.
oman.script: Arabic runs right to left and leaves most short vowels unwritten; Devanagari runs left to right and writes every vowel, so reading aloud is more predictable once the letters are learned.
oman.fl: Arabic speakers already make the kh, gh and q sounds that Urdu-flavoured Hindi uses and share vocabulary such as kitab, waqt and hukm.

pakistan.hook: From Lahore or Karachi the tutors are just half an hour ahead, so the whole teaching day — 8:30 in the morning to 9:30 at night — is usable for lessons.
pakistan.script: Urdu is written in Nastaliq, right to left; Devanagari writes the same spoken language left to right with every vowel marked. For Urdu speakers, the script is the main new skill.
pakistan.fl: Urdu speakers already speak most of everyday Hindi; the learning is in formal and written registers, where Hindi uses Sanskrit-derived words (for example vidyalaya for school) where Urdu uses Persian or Arabic ones.

palestine.dst: for part of the year from spring to autumn (UTC+3); the dates are set locally and can differ from Israel's
palestine.hook: Palestine is three and a half hours behind India in winter, and because its daylight-saving dates are set locally, it is especially worth letting the booking page read your own device's clock.
palestine.script: Arabic runs right to left; Devanagari runs left to right and writes every vowel, so it can be sounded out once the letters are learned.
palestine.fl: Arabic speakers share vocabulary that entered Hindi through Persian — kitab, duniya, waqt — and already produce the kh and gh sounds of Urdu-flavoured Hindi.

peru.hook: Peru stays at UTC-5 all year, ten and a half hours behind India, so the tutors' teaching day lands across Lima's night and early morning — best for early risers.
peru.script: Spanish and Quechua are written in Latin letters with regular spelling; Devanagari is just as regular, so once the letters are learned words are read exactly as written.
peru.fl: Spanish speakers already have pure vowels, a tapped r and unaspirated p, t and k, which Hindi uses; the new sounds are the aspirated and retroflex consonants.

philippines.hook: The Philippines is two and a half hours ahead of India at UTC+8, and Filipino itself carries a handful of Sanskrit loanwords from old trade routes — guro (teacher) and diwa (spirit) among them.
philippines.script: Filipino and English use the Latin alphabet; the old Baybayin script was a Brahmi-family abugida, the same kind of system as Devanagari.
philippines.fl: Filipino and English speakers find Hindi's vowels easy; the practice goes into retroflex and aspirated consonants and into putting the verb at the end of the sentence.

poland.dst: from the last Sunday of March to the last Sunday of October (UTC+2)
poland.hook: Poland is four and a half hours behind India in winter, which puts the Indian teaching day across Poland's morning and early afternoon, and Warsaw has a growing Indian tech community.
poland.script: Polish uses the Latin alphabet with diacritics for its extra sounds; Devanagari takes the same approach one step further, with a separate letter for every sound.
poland.fl: Polish speakers already distinguish consonant sounds that English merges, which helps with Hindi's four-way contrasts; Polish cases also prepare you for Hindi's postpositions.

qatar.hook: In Doha the tutors' day runs from 6:30 in the morning to 7:30 in the evening, so most learners in Qatar book either before work or straight after it.
qatar.script: Arabic runs right to left and omits most short vowels; Devanagari runs left to right and writes every vowel, a switch most learners manage within a few weeks.
qatar.fl: Arabic speakers already make the kh, gh and q sounds that Urdu-flavoured Hindi keeps and share words such as kitab, waqt and duniya.

romania.dst: from the last Sunday of March to the last Sunday of October (UTC+3)
romania.hook: Romania is three and a half hours behind India in winter, so the tutors' day covers Romania's morning and afternoon — a good fit for students and for people working remotely.
romania.script: Romanian is written in Latin letters with consistent spelling; Devanagari is consistent too, with vowels after a consonant written as attached marks.
romania.fl: Romanian speakers already have a rolled r and the neutral vowel ă, close to Hindi's short a; aspiration and retroflex consonants are the new sounds.

saudi-arabia.hook: In Riyadh and Jeddah a lesson can start at 6:30 in the morning and the last slots end around 7:30 in the evening, which fits around the Saudi working week.
saudi-arabia.script: Arabic runs right to left and leaves most short vowels unwritten; Devanagari runs left to right and writes every vowel, so reading aloud is predictable once the letters are learned.
saudi-arabia.fl: Arabic speakers share vocabulary that reached Hindi through Persian and already produce the kh, gh and q sounds of Urdu-flavoured Hindi.

singapore.hook: Singapore is two and a half hours ahead of India at UTC+8, and Hindi is one of the Indian languages its schools offer — many learners are Tamil- or English-speaking families adding Hindi.
singapore.script: Singaporeans who read Tamil already know a Brahmi-family script with the same consonant order and vowel signs; English and Chinese readers meet a phonetic system, far more regular than either.
singapore.fl: Tamil speakers share retroflex sounds with Hindi; Malay speakers know Sanskrit loanwords; English speakers lean on the English words in everyday Hindi.

south-africa.hook: South Africa's Indian community, much of it in KwaZulu-Natal, has roots going back to 1860, and Hindi is often a heritage language there; at UTC+2, South Africa is three and a half hours behind India.
south-africa.script: South African learners read a Latin alphabet; Devanagari is phonetic, so once the letters are learned words sound exactly as written.
south-africa.fl: Zulu and Xhosa speakers already distinguish aspirated consonants — an advantage for Hindi's kh/k and ph/p — and English speakers can lean on English loanwords.

sri-lanka.hook: Sri Lanka shares India's clock exactly — UTC+5:30 — so every lesson slot is the same time on both sides, and Hindi films and songs have long been popular there.
sri-lanka.script: Both Sinhala and Tamil scripts are Brahmi-family scripts, like Devanagari: the consonant order and vowel signs work the same way, so Devanagari is mostly new shapes for a familiar system.
sri-lanka.fl: Sinhala is an Indo-Aryan relative of Hindi with shared Sanskrit and Pali vocabulary, and Tamil speakers share Hindi's retroflex sounds.

syria.hook: Syria moved to permanent UTC+3 in 2022, two and a half hours behind India all year, and Indian films have had a large audience there for decades.
syria.script: Arabic runs right to left; Devanagari runs left to right and writes every vowel, so words can be sounded out once the letters are learned.
syria.fl: Arabic speakers already produce the kh, gh and q sounds that Urdu-flavoured Hindi keeps and share words such as kitab, waqt and duniya.

tajikistan.hook: In Dushanbe the tutors' teaching day runs from 8:30 in the morning to 9:30 at night, half an hour behind India, so almost any free hour can become a lesson.
tajikistan.script: Tajik is written in Cyrillic; Devanagari is an abugida, in which each consonant carries a vowel that small marks change.
tajikistan.fl: Tajik speakers have the largest vocabulary head start of any Central Asian learners, thanks to Persian; Russian speakers bring an ear for palatal consonants.

thailand.hook: Thailand is an hour and a half ahead of India at UTC+7, and Thai carries many Sanskrit and Pali words — phasa (language, Hindi bhasha) and racha (king, Hindi raja) among them.
thailand.script: The Thai script is a Brahmi-family script, like Devanagari: consonants in a related order and vowels written around them. Thai readers recognise the logic even where the shapes differ.
thailand.fl: Thai is tonal and Hindi is not, which learners find freeing; Thai speakers also already distinguish aspirated and unaspirated consonants, a real advantage for Hindi.

timor-leste.cur: the US dollar (USD), which Timor-Leste uses
timor-leste.hook: Timor-Leste is three and a half hours ahead of India at UTC+9 and uses the US dollar, so the lesson price needs no conversion at all.
timor-leste.script: Tetum and Portuguese are written in Latin letters; Devanagari is a different kind of system, in which each consonant carries a vowel that small marks change.
timor-leste.fl: Portuguese speakers already have nasal vowels, which Hindi uses in words like main and hain; the new sounds are retroflex and aspirated consonants.

turkiye.hook: In Istanbul the tutors' day runs from 6:30 in the morning to 7:30 in the evening all year, since Türkiye no longer changes its clocks.
turkiye.script: Turkish uses a phonetic Latin alphabet; Devanagari is phonetic too, one symbol per sound, so the principle is familiar even though the letters are new.
turkiye.fl: Turkish, like Hindi, puts the verb at the end and uses postpositions, so Hindi sentence structure feels natural to Turkish speakers.

turkmenistan.hook: Turkmenistan is half an hour behind India at UTC+5, so a lesson with a tutor in India lines up almost clock for clock.
turkmenistan.script: Turkmen is written in a Latin alphabet (Cyrillic before the 1990s); Devanagari is an abugida, in which each consonant carries a vowel that small marks change.
turkmenistan.fl: Turkmen puts the verb last and uses postpositions, as Hindi does, and shares some Persian vocabulary with it, so both sentence order and some words feel familiar.

uae.hook: In Dubai a lesson can start at 7:30 in the morning or finish at 8:30 in the evening, which suits learners who need Hindi for work and want to fit practice around shifts.
uae.script: Arabic runs right to left and leaves most short vowels unwritten; Devanagari runs left to right and writes every vowel.
uae.fl: Arabic speakers already make the kh, gh and q sounds of Urdu-flavoured Hindi, and many UAE residents have picked up spoken Hindi long before they take a lesson.

uk.dst: from the last Sunday of March to the last Sunday of October (BST, UTC+1)
uk.hook: From the UK the tutors' teaching day lands between 3:30 in the morning and 4:30 in the afternoon in winter, and an hour later in summer — so British learners usually book a morning or lunchtime lesson rather than an evening one.
uk.script: UK learners read a Latin alphabet; Devanagari is phonetic, so once its letters are learned every word can be read exactly as written — unlike English.
uk.fl: English speakers can lean on the many English words in everyday Hindi; the work is hearing aspirated and retroflex consonants, which English does not use to tell words apart.

usa.dst: from the second Sunday of March to the first Sunday of November (except Hawaii and most of Arizona)
usa.zones: The United States spans six main zones, from Eastern (UTC-5) to Hawaii (UTC-10); the figures here are Eastern Time, so subtract three hours on the Pacific coast.
usa.hook: The United States has the largest Indian diaspora in the world, and most American learners are either heritage speakers or partners in a Hindi-speaking family — booking across a ten-and-a-half-hour gap from the East Coast.
usa.script: American learners read a Latin alphabet; Devanagari is phonetic, so once the letters are learned words are read exactly as written — nothing like English spelling.
usa.fl: English speakers can lean on the English loanwords in everyday Hindi; the work is hearing aspirated and retroflex consonants, which English does not use to tell words apart.

uzbekistan.hook: In Tashkent a lesson can run from 8:30 in the morning to 9:30 at night, half an hour behind the tutor's clock, so fitting one around work or study is straightforward.
uzbekistan.script: Uzbek is officially written in a Latin alphabet, with Cyrillic still common; Devanagari is an abugida, in which each consonant carries a vowel that small marks change.
uzbekistan.fl: Uzbek puts the verb at the end and uses postpositions, as Hindi does, and shares Persian and Arabic vocabulary with it.

vietnam.hook: In Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City the tutors' teaching day runs from 10:30 in the morning to 11:30 at night, so an evening lesson after work is the easiest slot to find.
vietnam.script: Vietnamese uses a Latin alphabet with many diacritics for tones and vowels; Devanagari also adds marks to a base letter, but the marks change the vowel, not the pitch.
vietnam.fl: Vietnamese is tonal and Hindi is not; Vietnamese speakers already distinguish aspirated t from plain t, which helps with Hindi's aspirated consonants.

yemen.hook: In Yemen the tutors' day runs from 6:30 in the morning to 7:30 in the evening, all year round, with no clock changes on either side.
yemen.script: Arabic runs right to left; Devanagari runs left to right and writes every vowel, so words can be sounded out once the letters are learned.
yemen.fl: Arabic speakers share vocabulary that reached Hindi through Persian and already make the kh, gh and q sounds that Urdu-flavoured Hindi keeps.
